extracted.intended_audience: writers of fiction, novelists, literary students, and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for novelists on two contrasting narrative methods — the pictorial/panoramic mode and the dramatic/enacted mode — and how to manage point of view, scene selection, and the balance between them. Focuses on when to summarize and when to show, how to authenticate the narrator, and how to use chronology and detail for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial (panoramic) method
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreshortening and generalizing; fusion of detail; subordination of the instance and the occasion to the broad effect — sketching a train of life in broad free strokes (Thackeray’s panoramic/pictorial manner).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novelist uses scattered recollections, flashes and hints that arise as he reviews the past; these brief incidents illustrate and enrich the overall picture without full dramatization. This method enables coverage of great spaces of life and quantities of experience, producing vivid panoramas of manners, places, and time-pictures (e.g., Castlewood). Danger: it tends to make the omniscient author conspicuous and can leave the book with an inconclusive or thin look unless the point of view is authenticated or otherwise accounted for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic method (enactment/scene)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present action placed immediately before the reader — a piece of present action with which we are confronted; strictly dramatic and enacted by characters themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when the climax or decisive moment must be seen rather than summarized. Drama should be used for important occasions where direct enactment is required for proper emphasis. The dramatist-like scene lets characters declare themselves without continual authorial intervention; it is the novelist’s highest light and should be handled with circumspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use enacted scene for climactic answers rather than summary
rubrics_metrics.description: The final scene cannot be recalled and summarized in indirect, reminiscential manner; it must be placed immediately before us if it is to have proper emphasis and rightly round off a career or plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a central question of the story (e.g., 'Does Becky fail in the end?') requires a forceful answer, the plain and immediate performance of the answer — embodied in a scene that passes directly before us — gives the best possible warrant. Relying on retrospective account for such moments impairs their force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of drama — hoard dramatic enactment for important occasions
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama is the novelist’s highest light; to use it prodigally where it is not needed is to lessen its force where it is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve enacted scenes for significant episodes and climaxes. Overuse of scene-making in daily or familiar novels wastes its power; an economical procedure is to 'hoard it rather, reserving it for important occasions' so that when drama is required it has full impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticate or account for the narrator’s point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictorial method drags in the omniscient author and may make him exceedingly conspicuous; the mind and the eye that know the story must be made objective and accountable within the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid an 'inconclusive look' or a book that seems unfinished on one side, the novelist should dramatize the seeing eye or otherwise include the point of view in the story so it can be recognized and verified. When the narrator’s authority is accountable inside the fiction, the book feels complete and self-contained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend authorial vision with a character’s viewpoint (Flaubert’s method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Blend the acuter vision of the author with that of a character so that the character’s point of view seems to govern the story and the author’s intervention is unobtrusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flaubert’s technique — constantly mixing his vision with Emma’s so her point of view appears to govern — is recommended as a way for pictorial fiction to avoid making the narrator insistent; this makes authorial control discreet while preserving the panoramic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide ocular proof — show concrete moments to support narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Add brief enacted moments ('ocular proof') to lift and verify the narrated account — even a half-page scene can dramatize and substantiate an earlier summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, immediate scenes (e.g., Becky at the piano faced with hostility) provide 'ocular proof' that supplements the narrator’s account and makes the story more convincing. Such glimpses, though brief, add dramatic weight and clarity to narrated impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage continuity and manipulate chronology to convey time and atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Use leisurely play with chronology and shifting of focus so that time is stored up in description (time-pictures) rather than shown only as movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roam to and fro in narrative, delay and return over tracts of the past, shift the focal distance of scenes (far-away memory vs close presence) to create deep, tranquil senses of time. This is effective for producing the sensation of layered time rather than mere chronological sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and subordinate details to serve the broad effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Select hints, scraps of talk, and brief incidents that illustrate and enrich the picture without particularizing every scene; subordination of instance to broad effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brush past many incidents with a 'hint, a moment, a glance' sufficing for their contribution to the larger picture. Details should be fused and subordinated so the panoramic sweep remains dominant; use instances to enrich the stream rather than interrupt it with unnecessary dramatization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare characters sufficiently before demanding a dramatic performance
rubrics_metrics.description: If characters have not been rendered in immediate terms prior to an enacted scene, they may be forced to make an unnatural effort to meet dramatic requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sudden, belated dramatization that the novel’s prior method has not prepared for; instead render characters earlier with enough independence and life so when they 'come forward' to act they do so plausibly rather than artificially loud or theatrical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive repetition or negligent treatment of scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene is often neglected and yet recurs again and again in daily fiction, much too often, and its value is wasted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure every scene used contributes distinctively; do not repeat similar enacted moments that dilute impact. Treat scenes carefully and selectively so their dramatic value is not squandered by careless recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance picture and drama — skillful transitions and management of both methods
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist’s quality appears in his management of picture and drama: how he guides the story into the scene and how he picks it out of the scene to proceed with narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both methods as complements: panoramic narrative for breadth and drama for intensity. The art lies in choosing when to move from panorama to enactment and back, making the transitions purposeful so the story is richer and fuller than either method alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use earlier enacted scenes selectively to strengthen later catastrophe or contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow earlier triumphs or scenes to appear fully so subsequent disasters are strengthened by contrast and pre-existing clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A straightforward, unhampered view of an important earlier scene (e.g., a triumphal evening) would lend force to the impending catastrophe; missing such opportunities weakens the later dramatic effect and may force crude devices at the climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of panoramic thinness on rereading — make the work self-contained
rubrics_metrics.description: A book that relies heavily on the author’s panoramic presence may show a 'thinness' or inconclusive look when re-read unless the author’s role is integrated into the fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because books are separated from their authors when published, rely on internal means (dramatizing the seeing eye, including point of view) to make the narrative self-sufficient and avoid loose ends that draw attention away from the story itself.
